text: Lesson 19 treated a policy as a finished document. It isn't — a policy moves through a lifecycle, from first draft to eventual retirement, and skipping stages is exactly how organizations end up with rules nobody follows.

The first three stages: drafting, where the owner identifies the need and a steward authors a first controlled version naming its owner and a review date. Review, where legal, compliance, IT, and the governance committee assess accuracy and conflicts. And approval, where the committee approves, rejects, or sends it back for changes.

The next three: publication, getting the approved policy to the people actually expected to follow it, not just filed somewhere. Review and revision, triggered either by the scheduled date or by a real change. And retirement — formally removing an outdated policy from circulation.

Retirement is, in practice, the stage organizations handle worst. It's far easier to simply stop thinking about an old policy than to formally retire it — and the result is obsolete rules sitting next to current ones with no clear signal which is which. A lifecycle isn't complete until retirement gets the same formality as approval did.
Six stages, and retirement deserves just as much rigor as drafting did. Next lesson covers what actually makes a published policy matter day to day: policy enforcement. See you there.
